best: Found the single chokepoint (one AsyncOpenAI client per LLM config) and wrapped it there, so all five chat.completions sites route with no request-building changes: the outside check verifies 5/5 sites routing, 0 unverified, 0 not-routing, 20/20 live requests 200 including a Claude model via the Anthropic-compatible base URL, with the wrap inert until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 as a runtime revert.

Picked the right first lever for an agent loop and actually measured it: a ToolCallAgent step re-sends system prompt + full tool schemas every step, and the live cache probe (2,655-token request, 2,432 cached on the second call, $0.000398 -> $0.000216) is a real number with correct arithmetic, not an asserted percentage.

Read the failure path rather than just the happy path: caught that retry_if_exception_type((OpenAIError, Exception, ValueError)) matches everything and so contradicted its own 'Don't retry TokenLimitExceeded' comment (six retries, ~3 min, on an error raised before any HTTP call), fixed it with two new tests, and chose the fallback candidates against the runtime's capability guard (dropping temperature:false models like claude-sonnet-5) instead of guessing.
misses: No provider_timeout / retry-budget item, even though failover was built. The six tenacity attempts with up to 60 s exponential backoff survive untouched on all three user-waiting entry points; pairing a Router-only provider_timeout with a lower stop_after_attempt is the obvious companion to i2 and is the difference between 'failover in one request' and 'failover plus minutes of client-side backoff on top'. It appears only as a phrase inside the i5 rework item.

Left the migration's own blocking defect as a note instead of fixing it. config.example.toml names claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219, a non-catalog id, so the shipped configuration routes nothing even with the key set — the honest fix the report itself names (document catalog ids in the example configs) is a zero-risk one-line change that the engineer identified and then did not make, so 'all five call sites reach Router' is true of the code and not yet of any default deployment.

Nothing on the non-latency-sensitive half of the traffic or on context growth: no Flex-tier item for background/run_flow steps (Flex is named only inside the Responses-rewrite item, where it is gated behind a rewrite), and no item on the conversation history that each step re-sends — which is what makes agent-loop cost grow — nor on keying the cache per conversation/prefix rather than per feature label.
wrong: m1 overclaims deployment safety: unlock_hosts is derived from whatever base_url the operator set, and PPIO and Jiekou.AI are aggregators that serve catalog model ids (gpt-4o, claude-*). For those deployments the wrap does not 'behave exactly as before' — a catalog-id model silently moves off the operator's chosen aggregator onto Router, changing provider and bill with no opt-in beyond the key. The catalog-only guard protects Ollama and legacy ids, not OpenAI-id-shaped proxies; this risk is not stated anywhere.

i2's loss claim 'the response does not say which candidate served' is not a Router limitation — the response carries the model that answered; the gap is that app/llm.py does not log it. Stated as written it blames Router for an app-side omission, and it understates how cheap the fix is (log response.model).

i1 'loses: nothing' is too strong for a single prompt_cache_key per feature label. One key shared by every concurrent agent run means unrelated prefixes contend on the same affinity key, which can lower hit rate versus a per-conversation key; the measurement was a two-call single-session probe, which cannot show that effect.
Minor numeric slip in i4: gpt-4o-mini $0.15 -> gpt-5-nano $0.05 input is -67%, reported as 'about -60%'.

Both new test files write config/config.toml into the real checkout at collection time and delete it afterwards. It passes, but a test that mutates the operator's config directory is a side effect that should not ship in a migration's verification suite.

The check reports typecheck: {} and router requests 0/valid 0 for every branch, so the only automated evidence is the test counts (11 vs baseline 4) plus the engineer's own live runs; the report's per-item 'simulator pass / policy compiled' lines are self-reported and not corroborated by the outside check.
